items.title: Rucio: Unauthenticated administrator impersonation through SSH challenge tokens
items.description:
## Summary

SSH challenge tokens are mistakenly accepted as valid credentials during the authentication token validation process.

While an SSH challenge token is intended as a short-lived nonce for use in a subsequent SSH key exchange, the function to validate authentication tokens does not differentiate between these and actual authentication tokens. Because challenge tokens are generated based on an account name provided via headers without requiring prior authentication, an unauthenticated attacker can request a valid "challenge" token for any account (including administrative ones) and use it to authenticate against other API endpoints.

## Proof of Concept

items.title: Soup Sieve: Polynomial-time denial of service in the descendant combinator
items.description:
## Summary

Matching a selector that uses the descendant combinator (`a b`) takes time that grows polynomially with how deeply the document is nested, and each extra descendant combinator in the selector raises the degree by one. A selector with `k` descendant combinators takes `O(n^(k+1))` time on a chain of `n` nested elements.

An attacker who controls the HTML or XML that an application passes to Soup Sieve (directly, or through Beautiful Soup's `select()`, `select_one()`, `css.select()`, etc.) can send a very small, deeply nested document that keeps a CPU busy for seconds to minutes against an ordinary selector such as `section div div`.

## Details

items.title: Soup Sieve: General sibling combinator inside :has() matches untrusted HTML in quadratic time
items.description:
## Summary

Matching a selector that puts a general-sibling combinator inside `:has()`, such as `div:has(a ~ b)`, against untrusted HTML runs in O(n²) time in the number of sibling elements. A single small document with a few thousand siblings ties the process up for a minute of CPU, so an application that runs a fixed selector of this shape over HTML it doesn't control can be stalled by one request.

`:has` is powerful, but much in the same way poor regular expressions can be crafted to cause catastrophic backtracking with greedy capturing, has can be used to create non-ideal scenarios that can cause large portions of the tree to be evaluated for one or many elements if not used thoughtfully.

This behavior is not exclusive to Soup Sieve, but browsers make note of these potential performance issues themselves: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Selectors/:has#per

items.title: Active Storage: Possible arbitrary file write and read in image analysis
items.description:
### Impact
A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable by the application process. Those files typically include `secret_key_base` and credentials for external systems, which may in turn allow escalation to remote code execution or lateral movement to those systems.

### Details
ImageMagick selects a coder from the content of the file it is given, and some coders act on files named inside the image rather than on the image itself. Active Storage constrained none of ImageMagick's coders, and the ImageMagick analyzer runs when a file is attached, so an attacker who can upload a crafted file may be able to invoke one. Attaching the upload is sufficient; no variant, preview, or `analyze` call is required. One

items.title: Action Pack: Possible DoS vulnerability in Action Controller Live streaming
items.description:
### Impact
`ActionController::Live::Buffer#close` pushes its end-of-stream marker onto the response's bounded queue while it holds the buffer's monitor. When the client has stopped reading and the queue is full, the push blocks, and `Buffer#abort`, which runs when the client disconnects or a write times out, waits indefinitely for the same monitor. Each such response could permanently hold a web server thread and its `ActionController::Live` thread, possibly resulting in a DoS vulnerability through thread exhaustion.

Applications that stream responses with `ActionController::Live`, including `send_stream`, are affected. Applications that serve large files through Active Storage proxy mode are exposed to unauthenticated clients.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

items.title: Action Pack: Possible sensitive session information leak in Active Storage proxy mode
items.description:
### Impact
When `ActionDispatch::Cookies` reads a signed or encrypted cookie that was written under a rotated secret (`config.action_dispatch.cookies_rotations`) or in the format that a `:hybrid` cookie serializer migrates from, it writes the cookie back to the response in the current format, and that write ignores `request.session_options[:skip]`. `ActiveStorage::DisableSession` relies on that option to keep the session cookie off the public, immutable responses of the Active Storage proxy controllers, but those controllers still load the session, so a request carrying an old-format session cookie could receive the rewritten session cookie in `Set-Cookie` on a cacheable response. A shared cache that stores such a response together with its `Set-Cookie` header could then serve one user's session to later requesters of the same URL, or serve an attacker's session to other users.

items.title: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in highlight helper
items.description:
### Impact
`ActionView::Helpers::TextHelper#highlight` substitutes each matched phrase into the `:highlighter` string without escaping it and returns the result marked HTML-safe. Because sanitizing leaves quote characters in text unescaped, a match substituted into a quoted attribute value of the highlighter, such as the `<a href="search?q=\1">` form shown in the method's documentation, could end the attribute value and add attributes to the element, possibly leading to XSS. Applications are affected when they pass a `:highlighter` that places a placeholder inside an attribute value and highlight text or phrases that a user controls. The default `<mark>\1</mark>` highlighter and the block form are not affected.

### Details
The fixed releases HTML-escape each group substituted into the `:highlighter` string, so quotes in a match are rendered as `"` and `'`. Only the numbered pla

items.title: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in strip_tags
items.description:
### Impact
`strip_tags` in Action View returns its sanitized output marked `html_safe`, but the underlying sanitizer encodes only `&`, `<` and `>`, leaving `"` and `'` unencoded. Because ERB does not escape a string marked `html_safe`, untrusted input passed through `strip_tags` and rendered inside a quoted HTML attribute value could close the attribute and add new attributes, possibly leading to XSS. Applications that render `strip_tags` output from untrusted input inside an HTML attribute, for example in a `title` attribute or a `<meta content>` tag, are affected. Output rendered as element content is not affected.

### Details
`strip_tags` now encodes `"` and `'` in its output, as well as `&`, `<` and `>`, without double-encoding existing entities. Applications that use `strip_tags` output outside HTML, such as in a text template or JSON, now see `"` and `'` where they saw `"

items.title: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in text helpers
items.description:
### Impact
With the HTML5 sanitizer (`Rails::HTML5::Sanitizer`, the default vendor on CRuby for applications using `load_defaults 7.1` or later), Nokogiri before 1.19.5 serializes `<` and `>` unescaped inside attribute values. The Action View text helpers `highlight` and `simple_format` sanitize their input and then process the resulting HTML as a string: `highlight` splits it on tag boundaries to insert matches, and `simple_format` splits it into paragraphs on blank lines. An unescaped `>` or a blank line inside an attribute value could cause markup in that value, which the sanitizer left inert, to be emitted as live elements in the helper's `html_safe` output, possibly leading to XSS. Applications that use the HTML5 sanitizer and pass untrusted text to `highlight`, or to `simple_format` with `html_options`, are affected.

### Details
The fixed releases require rails-html-sanitizer 1.7.

items.title: Active Storage: Unsigned Content-Type in GCS direct uploads with cache_control
items.description:
### Impact
When a GCS service is configured with the `cache_control` option, `ActiveStorage::Service::GCSService#url_for_direct_upload` signs direct-upload URLs with V4, and the V4 signature covers only the `Cache-Control` and `Host` headers. A direct-upload client can therefore send a `Content-Type` of its choosing, and can omit the declared `Content-MD5`, without invalidating the URL. GCS stores the supplied content type as object metadata, which takes precedence over the `response-content-type` that Active Storage sets on download URLs, so an uploaded object could be served as inline HTML under the application's bucket path on `storage.googleapis.com`. Script in such an object runs on the storage origin rather than the application's, but could register a Service Worker scoped to the bucket path and read or replace a victim's later responses for signed URLs in that bucket.

items.title: Action Pack: Possible Strong Parameters Bypass in Parameters#each_key
items.description:
### Impact
`ActionController::Parameters#each_key` delegates to the internal `ActiveSupport::HashWithIndifferentAccess` that holds the request parameters, so when called with a block it returns that hash instead of the `Parameters` instance. The hash does not respond to `permitted?`, so Active Model mass assignment (`new`, `assign_attributes`, `update`) accepts it without raising `ActiveModel::ForbiddenAttributesError`. An application that passes the return value of `each_key` to mass assignment could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to set attributes that the application does not permit, such as an authorization flag.

This is an incomplete fix of [CVE-2020-8164](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8727-m6gj-mc37), which made `each`, `each_pair` and `each_value` return the `Parameters` instance but left `each_key` delegated.

### Details

items.title: Hono: `csrf()` does not check requests sent by hyperlink auditing (`text/ping`)
items.description:
### Summary

`csrf()` validates a request only when its `Content-Type` is one of the three types an HTML form can send. Chromium's hyperlink auditing (`<a ping>`) sends a cross-origin POST with the user's cookies and the content type `text/ping`, which is not in that list. The middleware does not look at `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` for such a request, so it is passed to the handler.

### Details

The middleware skips the origin check when the content type is not one that a form submission produces. The assumption was that any other content type requires a CORS preflight and therefore cannot be sent cross-origin with credentials. Hyperlink auditing is an exception: Chrome and Edge send the ping as a credentialed POST without a preflight, with a fixed body and `Content-Type: text/ping`.

A page on another origin can therefore trigger a POST to any URL of the application. The `csrf()` opti

items.title: Hono: `validator('form')` skips validation for `multipart/form-data` requests with extra parameters
items.description:
### Summary

`validator('form')` only recognizes a `multipart/form-data` `Content-Type` that carries nothing but a single `boundary` parameter. A request with another legal parameter, such as `charset`, or with extra whitespace after the `;` is not recognized as a form. The validation callback then receives an empty object, while `c.req.parseBody()` still parses the body as a form.

### Details

The check that decides whether a request body is a form was written as a strict pattern over the whole `Content-Type` value. Any parameter list that does not look exactly like `; boundary=...` fails the check. When it fails, the middleware does not read the body and passes an empty object to the validation callback. If the callback accepts an empty object, the request proceeds to the handler, which can still read all submitted fields through `c.req.parseBody()` or `c.req.formData()`.

items.title: Hono: `mount()` and `app.mount()` can forward a path that bypasses middleware scoped inside the mount prefix
items.description:
### Summary

`mount()` and `app.mount()` remove the mount prefix from the request path and forward the rest to the mounted application. Two mistakes in that step let a crafted request reach a route of the mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware, such as an authentication check on `/app/admin/*`. The outer application routes on the original path, so the middleware does not run.

### Details

1. **Dynamic prefix** (all affected versions): for a mount such as `/api/:tenant/*`, the prefix was removed by the length of the route pattern, not of the matched prefix. A request with a longer or shorter first segment is cut in the middle, so `/api/a/xxxxx/admin/secret` reaches the mounted application as `/admin/secret`.
2. **Re-normalization** (since 4.12.21): the forwarded path was built from the decoded request path and assigned to `url.pathname`, which

items.title: Hono: RegExpRouter skips wildcard middleware for some route sets and for paths with an encoded line terminator
items.description:
### Summary

RegExpRouter, which the default `SmartRouter` selects for most applications, skipped wildcard middleware in three cases, so a route handler ran without the middleware registered for it:

1. Middleware whose parameter is written with the explicit default pattern, such as `/api/:tenant{[^/]+}/admin/*`, was not applied to a route written as `/api/:tenant/admin/:id`. (since 4.13.0)
2. Middleware on `/admin/*` was not applied to a route registered on `/admin*` for paths under `/admin/`. (since 4.1.4)
3. For a path with an encoded line terminator (`%0A`, `%0D`, `%E2%80%A8`, `%E2%80%A9`), no wildcard pattern matched, so the request reached the not-found handler without any wildcard middleware. (since 4.4.0)

TrieRouter, LinearRouter and PatternRouter apply the middleware in all three cases.

items.title: Hono: `css` helper does not escape a closing tag split between the template and an interpolated value, allowing HTML injection
items.description:
### Summary

The `css` helper in `hono/css` escapes a `/` that follows `<` inside an interpolated value so that a value cannot close the `<style>` element. The check only looks inside each value. When the text before a value ends with `<`, whether that is the template itself or an earlier interpolated value, and the next value starts with `/`, the `/` is not escaped and the combined output contains an unescaped closing tag.

### Details

Interpolated string values are escaped one at a time before they are joined with the surrounding template text. The rule that neutralizes `</` therefore cannot see a `<` that belongs to the template. A template such as a `content` declaration that opens with a literal `<` and interpolates a string right after it produces a raw `</style>` when that string starts with `/style>`. items.title: @grpc/grpc-js: safe_regex incorrectly applies partial string matching for patterns with alternation
items.description:
### Summary

The StringMatcher/PathMatcher for `safe_regex` builds its RE2 as `^${regex}$` with no surrounding group. Because alternation has the lowest precedence, a pattern `"a|b|c"` compiles to `/^a|b|c$/` -- "starts with a" OR "contains b" OR "ends with c" instead of a full match of the whole value. Configurations with `safe_regex` matchers that use a regex alternation (a natural way to list methods or service identities) therefore apply partial string matches. This impacts route selection, xDS credentials, and RBAC.

### Details

`src/matcher.ts`: `SafeRegexValueMatcher` and `PathSafeRegexValueMatcher` both do
```ts
this.targetRegexImpl = new RE2(`^${targetRegex}$`, 'u');
```

and `apply()` returns `targetRegexImpl.test(value)`. With a top-level alternation the anchors bind only to the first/last branch.

items.title: msgpack-ruby JRuby decoder makes uncapped header-count allocations; a 5-byte message forces multi-GiB OOM
items.description:
### Summary

The **JRuby** implementation of msgpack (`msgpack` gem, `java` platform — pure Java decoder under `ext/java/`) sizes containers directly from the element count written in the message header, with **no cap at all**: no equivalent of the C unpacker's `SHRT_MAX` clamp (since 1.7.3) and none of the buffered-bytes cap that commit c8d42d8 added for CRuby in 1.8.6. A single 5-byte message decides how much memory a JVM process tries to allocate:

* `array32` header declaring `0x7FFFFFFF` elements → `new IRubyObject[0x7FFFFFFF]` (~8 GiB of reference slots) attempted immediately → `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit`.
* Counts *below* the VM's max-array-size but above available heap (e.g. 5×10⁸ with a 512 MiB heap) produce a **real allocation attempt** — `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` — the JVM genuinely tries to take the memory before failing.

items.title: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts with invalid Punycode A-labels
items.description:
### Impact

`Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode`, in the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning with `xn--`) that are not valid A-labels. Those labels are returned in decoded form, when they should be returned unchanged. That includes:

- labels that decode to only ASCII characters, e.g. `xn--google-` decodes to `google`;
- labels that decode to text that doesn't convert back to the same label (RFC 3490 §4.2), e.g. text that isn't in normalized form.

`Addressable::URI#display_uri` uses `to_unicode`, so for `https://xn--google-.example.org/` it displays the host `google.example.org`, while `#host`, `#normalized_host` and any connection made from the URI use `xn--google-.example.org`. An attacker who controls a domain can therefore have a URI displayed as a host they don't control. Applications that compare the result of `to_unicode` against a list of trusted n

items.title: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts containing bidi and invisible characters
items.description:
### Impact

`Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode` decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning with `xn--`) that contain characters which change how text is displayed without being visible themselves. These include bidirectional controls such as U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE and U+2066–U+2069, zero-width characters, and other invisible format characters. `Addressable::URI#display_uri` uses `to_unicode`, so it can display a host whose characters appear reordered or which looks identical to a different host. For example, the host of `http://xn--abcmoc-dm0c.com/` is displayed as `abc`, U+202E, `moc.com`, and the override makes everything after `abc` render right to left.

Parsing, `host`, `normalized_host` and any connection made from the URI are not affected. Only the displayed form is. Applications that show `display_uri` to users (link previews, chat and email clients, admin interfaces) can be use

items.title: Addressable: Denial of service in URI path normalization
items.description:
### Impact

`Addressable::URI.normalize_path` takes time quadratic in the number of nested dot segments in a path (e.g., `"/" + "a/" * n + "../" * n`, which for n = 3 is `/a/a/a/../../../`), because it removes one dot segment per pass over the whole path. `URI#normalize`, `URI#normalized_path`, `URI#==`, `URI#===` and `URI#join` all call it. Normalizing, comparing or joining a URI taken from user input can result in uncontrolled resource consumption, leading to denial of service. On 2.9.0, normalizing a 34 KB path takes about 3.5 seconds on MRI Ruby 4.0, and the cost grows with the square of the path length.

This affects every Ruby implementation, including MRI Ruby 3.2 and later. `URI.parse` by itself is unaffected, as is code that never normalizes, compares, or joins URIs from untrusted sources.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects all versions of Addressable prior to 2.

items.title: Addressable: Regular Expression Denial of Service in templates with certain exploded expressions
items.description:
### Impact

Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates using the `*` (explode) modifier with the `/`, `.`, `;`, `?` or `&` operators (e.g., `{/segments*}`, `{.ext*}`, `{;params*}`, `{?query*}`) generate regular expressions vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking. When `Template#match` or `Template#extract` is called with a maliciously crafted URI that starts with the operator's leading character, matching takes exponential time, leading to uncontrolled resource consumption and denial of service. An input under 60 bytes is enough to occupy a thread for minutes.

GHSA-h27x-rffw-24p4 (CVE-2026-35611) reported this pattern as fully remediated in 2.9.0. The 2.9.0 fix only made the joiner between exploded members mandatory for templates without an operator, and its regression specs used inputs that never start with the operator's leading character, so the vulnerable part

items.title: Addressable: Regular Expression Denial of Service in templates with multiple variables
items.description:
### Impact

Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates that put several variables in one expression generate regular expressions vulnerable to excessive backtracking:

1. Expressions with any operator other than `+` and `#` (e.g., `{/owner,repo,ref}`, `{.a,b}`, `{a,b,c}`, `{;a,b,c}`). The values are joined by an optional separator, so a run of characters can be divided among the variables in O(n^k) ways for k variables.
2. Expressions with the `+` or `#` operators and many variables (e.g., `{+v1,v2,v3,v4,v5,v6,v7,v8,v9,v10}`). A failing match is exponential in the number of variables.
3. Several single-variable expressions next to each other (e.g., `{+a}{+b}{+c}` or `{a}{b}{c}`), which are polynomial in the input length.

items.title: Addressable URI normalization resolves some dotted path segments to the wrong path
items.description:
### Summary

`Addressable::URI.normalize_path` resolves some paths containing `..` segments to a different path than RFC 3986 does. When a path climbs above the root before any other `..` is resolved, the segments that later `..` segments should remove are instead kept: `/../../public/x/../../secret` normalizes to `/public/x/secret` instead of `/secret`. `URI#normalize`, `URI#join`, `URI#==` and `URI#===` all use this normalization. An application that checks a normalized Addressable path against an allowlist, but sends the original URI to something that resolves it according to RFC 3986, can be made to allow a request for a path outside the allowlist.

### Details

`normalize_path` in 2.9.0 (`lib/addressable/uri.rb`) removes dot segments by repeating a set of rewrites until nothing changes. On each pass it finds the first `/segment/../` pair with `RULE_2B_2C`, then replaces every textua

items.title: basic-ftp: Uncaught exception crashes the Node.js process when a password (or resumed-download path) contains CR/LF
Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in tag helpers
items.description:
### Impact
The fix for [CVE-2026-33168](https://github.com/rails/rails/security/advisories/GHSA-v55j-83pf-r9cq) skips blank HTML attribute names in Action View tag helpers, but it tests the name before converting it to a string. A Symbol name made only of whitespace, such as `:" "`, is not blank, because `Symbol#blank?` is `Symbol#empty?`, so it reaches the attribute escaping, which emits an attribute with no name and produces malformed HTML. The asset tag helpers, such as `image_tag`, `video_tag` and `audio_tag`, symbolize their options, so a whitespace String name passed to them takes the same path. A carefully crafted attribute value could then be misinterpreted by the browser as a separate attribute name, possibly leading to XSS. Applications that allow users to specify custom HTML attribute names are affected.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

items.title: Active Storage: Possible local file disclosure in video previews and analysis
items.description:
### Impact
Active Storage's `VideoPreviewer`, `VideoAnalyzer` and `AudioAnalyzer` run `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` on a blob's contents without restricting the input format, so FFmpeg selects a demuxer by probing the file. A blob created through a direct upload keeps the content type the client declared, so a client can store an HLS playlist under a `video/*` or `audio/*` type. When that blob is previewed or analyzed, the `hls` demuxer opens the `file://` segments that the playlist names, and the preview image or the stored metadata could disclose a local media file that the application process can read and whose path the attacker knows.

Applications that accept uploads from untrusted users and generate video previews, or analyze video or audio attachments with FFmpeg, are affected.

### Details
The fixed releases limit the formats FFmpeg may open to common audio and video containers, configu

items.title: basic-ftp: Uncaught TypeError in MLSD directory-listing parser via __proto__ fact name causes DoS in Client.list()
items.description:
### Summary

basic-ftp's MLSD directory-listing parser (src/parseListMLSD.ts) looks up fact-handler functions in a plain object literal keyed directly by fact names taken from the FTP server's response, with no validation. A directory-listing line containing the fact name "__proto__" resolves this lookup to Object.prototype (inherited, non-own, non-function) instead of undefined, so the "not a function" guard is bypassed and the code throws `TypeError: factHandler is not a function`.

This TypeError is not an FTPError, so it is not caught by Client.list()'s retry logic and propagates as a rejected promise out of list() and every API built on top of it (list, downloadToDir, uploadFromDir, clearWorkingDir, removeDir). items.title: @hono/node-server: Unhandled `ECONNRESET` on the socket during an asynchronous WebSocket upgrade crashes the process
items.description:
### Summary

While `@hono/node-server` waits for the Hono application to handle a WebSocket upgrade request, the socket has no error listener. If the client resets the TCP connection during that time, the resulting `ECONNRESET` is emitted as an unhandled `'error'` event and the process terminates.

### Details

The upgrade handler awaits the application before attaching any listener to the socket. When middleware on the upgrade path does asynchronous work, such as an authentication lookup, a connection reset in that window has no handler. If a global `uncaughtException` handler swallows the error, the pending upgrade is never released and its entry is retained for the lifetime of the process.

The fix attaches error and close listeners to the socket before calling the application, releases the pending upgrade when the socket closes, and skips the handshake on a destroyed socket.

items.title: @hono/node-server: Backslash in the request path is parsed as a path separator, bypassing path-based access control at a reverse proxy
items.description:
### Summary

`@hono/node-server` passes the raw request-target to the WHATWG URL parser, which treats a backslash in the path as `/` and then resolves `..` segments. A request for `/admin\secret` or `/public\..\admin/secret` reaches the application as `/admin/secret`. A reverse proxy that follows RFC 3986 forwards the backslash unchanged and applies its path-based rules to the original path, so the request reaches a route the proxy is meant to block.

### Details

A raw backslash is not allowed in a request-target (RFC 3986, RFC 9112 Section 3.2.1), and RFC 9112 Section 3.2 says a recipient should reject such a request rather than correct it. Proxies such as nginx on Linux, HAProxy and Envoy keep the backslash as an ordinary character, so they and the application see different paths.

items.title: Loofah: SVG `<textPath>` and `<mpath>` bypass local-reference restriction
items.description:
## Summary

Loofah restricts `href` and `xlink:href` on certain SVG elements to same-document references. Two elements escaped the restriction:

- `<textPath>`: `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF` listed it in lowercase as `textpath`, but the HTML5 parser names the element `textPath` inside `<svg>`, so the check never matched on the HTML5 path.
- `<mpath>`: absent from `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF`, so its references were never restricted on either path.

`rails-html-sanitizer` reuses this safelist in its `PermitScrubber`, so it is affected too.

## Impact

An external `href` or `xlink:href` on `<textPath>` or `<mpath>` survives sanitization. Firefox fetches the URL when rendering the content, which leaks the viewer's IP address, user agent, and referrer, and can reach hosts routable only from the viewer's network. items.title: Loofah allowed_uri? treats javascript&#x3a alert(1) as safe
items.description:
## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` returns `true` for a `javascript:` or `vbscript:` URI whose scheme is split by a numeric character reference without a trailing semicolon, followed by a character that `allowed_uri?` strips, such as a space or tab. A browser ends the reference at that character and reads `javascript&#x3a alert(1)` as `javascript: alert(1)`.

## Details

`allowed_uri?` strips control characters and whitespace before it decodes numeric character references. Removing the character that ends a semicolon-less reference lets the reference run on into the following text, so `&#x3a alert` decodes as `&#x3aa` (U+03AA) instead of a colon, and no scheme is detected. The same applies to decimal references and to references that encode a scheme letter, as in `&#x6a\tavascript:alert(1)`.

items.title: Loofah: CSS url() sanitization bypass via escaped parentheses
items.description:
## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.scrub_css` rejected any property whose top-level Crass tokens included a `:url` or `:bad_url`, and left `url` out of the allowed CSS functions. Both checks ran only against the first parse of the `style` attribute. When `scrub_css` rebuilt each property it emitted identifiers with their CSS escapes decoded, so parentheses written as escapes — `url\28 …\29` — hid the `url` token from the checks, and the rebuilt value was re-parsed into a live `url()` that nothing checked again. An escaped property name, six-digit escapes, escaped comments and escaped quotes all reached the same place.

## Impact

items.title: Loofah: Regular expression denial of service in the SVG local-reference check
items.description:
## Summary

Loofah's HTML5 sanitizer restricts the `href` and `xlink:href` attributes of SVG reference elements to local references. That check matched the attribute value against `/^\s*[^#\s].*/m`. In Ruby `^` anchors to every line start and `\s` matches newlines, so an all-whitespace value made the engine rescan the value from each of its line starts, taking time quadratic in its length.

Only Ruby 3.1 and earlier are affected. Ruby 3.2 added linear-time regexp matching, which makes the pattern linear.

## Impact

An attacker who supplies HTML to be sanitized can consume CPU out of proportion to the input size, by sending an SVG reference element whose `href` or `xlink:href` is a long run of whitespace.

The default safelist allows the elements in `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF`, so no configuration change is required.

items.description:
## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` returns `true` for a `data:` URI whose mediatype is written with the HTML5 named character reference `/` in place of the solidus. Loofah reads that mediatype as malformed and falls back to the allowed `text/plain`, while a browser decodes the reference and reads the same URI as `text/html`.

`allowed_uri?` decodes HTML entities with `CGI.unescapeHTML`, which handles numeric character references but not HTML5 named character references. `/` therefore survives normalization, so the mediatype carries no `/`, fails the MIME grammar, and falls back to the allowed `text/plain` under the WHATWG rule for a malformed mediatype.

items.title: Loofah: Mutation XSS in the HTML5 scrubbers through unescaped attribute values
items.description:
## Summary

Loofah's HTML5 scrubbers could emit output that a browser parses into different markup, allowing mutation XSS. Nokogiri < 1.19.5 did not escape `<` and `>` in attribute values. When the output contained certain MathML, a browser treated markup inside an allowed attribute as live HTML. The `:strip` scrubber is affected in every browser. The `:prune` and `:escape` scrubbers are affected in WebKit browsers such as Safari.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 escapes `<` and `>` in attribute values, as the HTML standard requires. Loofah 2.25.3 requires Nokogiri >= 1.19.5.

## Impact

Applications that sanitize untrusted HTML with Loofah's HTML5 API (`Loofah.html5_fragment`, `Loofah.html5_document` and the `scrub_html5_*` methods) and display the result to other people are affected, including with the default allowlist.

items.title: pgEdge Control Plane generates pg_hba.conf with trust authentication for local and loopback connections
items.description:
### Summary

Every `pg_hba.conf` generated by the pgEdge Control Plane begins with a hard-coded block of `trust` entries covering Unix-socket and loopback connections. Any operating-system account that can reach the Postgres socket or the loopback interface on a database host can authenticate as any Postgres role, including the superuser, without presenting a credential.

### Details

The generated file opens with the following six entries:

host    all         all     127.0.0.1/32    trust
host    all         all     ::1/128         trust
local   replication all                     trust
host    replication all     127.0.0.1/32    trust
host    replication all     ::1/128         trust
```

items.title: pgEdge RAG Server unbounded corpus read allows resource exhaustion from unauthenticated requests
items.description:
### Impact

An unauthenticated caller able to reach the query endpoint could exhaust database and server resources with ordinary, inexpensive requests.

The keyword-search arm read the entire corpus on every request and rebuilt an in-memory BM25 index from it, so the cost of serving a query scaled with the size of the source table rather than with the size of the result set. Each request cost the server and the tenant's database far more than it cost the caller to make, which makes this a materially more effective denial-of-service lever than flooding the endpoint with ordinary requests. The amplification factor grows with corpus size, so the largest deployments are the most exposed.

items.title: pgEdge RAG Server discloses part of the configured provider credential through API error messages
items.description:
### Impact

An unauthenticated remote caller could read part of the operator's configured LLM provider API key.

The query API relayed the text of a provider error straight to the caller. That text carried the upstream provider's own message, and providers characteristically quote a partially masked form of the credential they rejected when authentication fails — so a failing provider call published a fragment of the operator's key. A caller who can reach the endpoint can cause such a failure and read the result.

**Who is affected:** any deployment of pgEdge RAG Server at `1.0.0` or earlier, including all alpha and beta pre-releases, whose query endpoint was reachable by an untrusted party. The endpoint carries no authentication in the affected versions.

items.title: pgEdge RAG Server shared keyword index leaked results between concurrent unauthenticated requests
items.description:
### Impact

Documents belonging to one caller could be returned to another. Where an application passes a customer or tenant identifier as a search filter, that scoping could be defeated by ordinary concurrent traffic. **No injection and no malformed input are required** — normal load is enough.

The BM25 keyword index was a single per-pipeline object shared by every request. A request cleared it, refilled it from its own filtered corpus and then searched it, taking a separate lock for each step rather than holding the sequence as a unit. Concurrent requests therefore interleaved, and a search could run against a corpus that a different request's filter had populated.

**Who is affected:** any deployment of pgEdge RAG Server at `1.0.0` or earlier, including all alpha and beta pre-releases, that serves concurrent queries — most acutely those relying on a search filter to separate tenants

items.title: Signal K Server: Buffered logs exposed to unauthenticated WebSocket clients
code16/sharp: Server-side request forgery through an unanchored autocomplete endpoint check
items.description:
### Impact
An authenticated attacker can call the Autocomplete API with the configured endpoint as a substring to request another server-side route.

### Patches
The problem has been patched in 9.23.0 and pre-release version 10.0.0-beta.4. The regex verifying the endpoint has been anchored to forbid substring injection.

### Workarounds
Use `SharpFormAutocompleteRemoteField::setRemoteCallback()` instead of `SharpFormAutocompleteRemoteField::setRemoteEndpoint()`.

items.title: code16/sharp: Arbitrary class instantiation through the embed_key API parameter
items.description:
### Impact

An authenticated attacker can instantiate any class in the PHP application by using the `embed_key` parameter across multiple API endpoints. The instantiation is performed by the Laravel container. As a result, the `__construct()` method of the class is called and all constructor dependencies are resolved. The attacker cannot specify parameter values and cannot call any arbitrary method.

### Patches

The problem has been patched in 9.23.0 and pre-release version 10.0.0-beta.4. An additional check was added to verify that `embed_key` is a class extending `SharpFormEditorEmbed` before any instantiation.

### Workarounds

No known workarounds.

items.title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-114155 - .NET Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability
items.description:
## Executive summary

Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in the .NET SDK's dotnet-watch component. This advisory provides guidance on updating affected SDK installations.

A local attacker who can replace or modify a temporary solution file used by dotnet-watch can alter a subsequent build. The fix stores generated solution files in a private temporary directory and keeps each file open with read-only sharing while the build uses it.

## Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/502
